usamts-2020-r2-01.title: Use the bounds on each gray cell
usamts-2020-r2-01.body:
Number rows $1$–$6$ from the top and columns $1$–$7$ from the left. The gray cells are $(1,4)$, $(2,2)$, $(2,6)$, $(3,4)$, $(3,6)$, $(4,2)$, $(5,4)$, $(5,6)$, $(6,2)$.

**Size of each sum.** Since the digits around a gray cell are distinct, a gray cell touching $w$ white cells has a sum between $1 + 2 + \dots + w$ and $9 + 8 + \dots + (10 - w)$. For instance $(1,4)$ (top edge) touches only $5$ white cells, and $(6,2)$ (bottom edge) touches only $5$; $(2,6)$ and $(3,6)$ each touch another gray cell. The given digits fix part of each sum. The smallest bank number $15$ must go to a cell with few white neighbours, and the large numbers $42$, $44$ to cells with $8$ (or $7$) white neighbours.

**Matching.** Working through the cells with the most given digits first and matching the remaining sums against the bank yields
$$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|}\hline 8 & 5 & 1 & \mathbf{15} & 5 & 8 & 9\\\hline 4 & \mathbf{38} & 2 & 3 & 4 & \mathbf{35} & 2\\\hline 6 & 3 & 9 & \mathbf{44} & 6 & \mathbf{28} & 1\\\hline 4 & \mathbf{40} & 7 & 8 & 5 & 7 & 3\\\hline 1 & 8 & 2 & \mathbf{42} & 1 & \mathbf{36} & 4\\\hline 3 & \mathbf{23} & 9 & 4 & 6 & 2 & 8\\\hline\end{array}$$
**Check** (sum of the touching white cells, all terms distinct):

* $(1,4)$: $1 + 5 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 15$
* $(2,2)$: $8 + 5 + 1 + 4 + 2 + 6 + 3 + 9 = 38$
* $(2,6)$: $5 + 8 + 9 + 4 + 2 + 6 + 1 = 35$
* $(3,4)$: $2 + 3 + 4 + 9 + 6 + 7 + 8 + 5 = 44$
* $(3,6)$: $4 + 2 + 6 + 1 + 5 + 7 + 3 = 28$
* $(4,2)$: $6 + 3 + 9 + 4 + 7 + 1 + 8 + 2 = 40$
* $(5,4)$: $7 + 8 + 5 + 2 + 1 + 9 + 4 + 6 = 42$
* $(5,6)$: $5 + 7 + 3 + 1 + 4 + 6 + 2 + 8 = 36$
* $(6,2)$: $1 + 8 + 2 + 3 + 9 = 23$

Each bank number is used once. (A computer search confirms this is the only solution.)

**Answer:** the grid above.

usamts-2020-r2-02.title: A beast at the front always has a helper with candy behind
usamts-2020-r2-02.body:
**$n = 1$ and $n = 2$ work.** For $n = 1$ the beast behind Grogg receives the only piece. For $n = 2$, beasts $2$ and $3$ (numbering by original position, Grogg $= 1$) get one piece each; then beast $2$ passes its piece to beast $3$, who now holds both.

**$n \ge 3$ fails.** After Grogg passes, beasts $2, \dots, n + 1$ hold one piece each; after beast $2$ passes, beast $3$ holds $2$ and beasts $4, \dots, n+1$ hold one each.

*Claim:* for $s \ge 3$, when beast $s$ reaches the front it holds at least $2$ pieces and beast $s + 1$ holds at least $1$. True for $s = 3$ (as $n \ge 3$, beast $4$ has a piece). If it holds for $s$, beast $s$ passes one piece to each of beasts $s + 1$ and $s + 2$ (it has at least two pieces), so beast $s + 1$ then has at least $1 + 1 = 2$ and beast $s + 2$ at least $1$. $\square$

Now check every moment. Beast $2$ never holds more than $1 < n$ pieces. Whenever beast $s \ge 3$ is at the front, beast $s + 1$ also has candy, so neither holds everything; and while a beast is passing, it gives pieces to at least two different beasts (or still holds some itself), so nobody holds all the candy then either. Beasts never hold candy before they are reached by passing from someone in front, and the front beast always shares with at least one other.

**Answer: $n = 1$ and $n = 2$**

usamts-2020-r2-02.title: The candy amounts never increase toward the back
usamts-2020-r2-02.body:
Suppose some beast $L \ne$ Grogg holds all the candy, and look at the moment just before (between two complete passing turns). By the rules, at that earlier moment:

* $L$ is not at the front (she would leave);
* at most one beast $W$ besides $L$ has candy, and $W$ is at the front with at least one piece (otherwise the next turn could not concentrate all candy at $L$);
* $L$ stands right behind $W$, and $W$ has exactly $1$ piece (more pieces would also reach the beast behind $L$). So $W$ has $1$ and $L$ has $n - 1$.

**Lemma.** Between turns, the amounts held from the front of the line to the back are non-increasing. *Proof by induction:* initially only Grogg has candy. If the amounts are $a_1 \ge a_2 \ge \dots$, the front beast adds $1$ to each of the next $a_1$ beasts, giving $a_2 + 1 \ge \dots \ge a_{a_1 + 1} + 1 \ge a_{a_1 + 2} \ge \dots$, still non-increasing. $\square$

So $1 \ge n - 1$, i.e. $n \le 2$. Together with the examples, the answer is $n \in \{1, 2\}$.

**Answer: $n = 1, 2$**

usamts-2020-r2-03.title: Compare the two top coefficients
usamts-2020-r2-03.body:
By Vieta, a polynomial $c_dx^d + c_{d-1}x^{d-1} + \dots$ (with $c_d \ne 0$, $d \ge 1$) has $S = -\frac{c_{d-1}}{c_d}$. So
$$p(x) = ax^n - 7ax^{n-1} + \cdots,\qquad q(x) = bx^m - 9bx^{m-1} + \cdots$$
with $a, b \ne 0$.

**The degrees differ by at most $1$.** If $n \ge m + 2$, then $p - q$ begins $ax^n - 7ax^{n-1}$, so $S(p - q) = 7 \ne 11$. Similarly $m \ge n + 2$ gives $S(p - q) = 9$. So $|n - m| \le 1$.

* **$n = m$.** $p - q = (a - b)x^n - (7a - 9b)x^{n-1} + \cdots$.
  * If $a = b$, then $p + q = 2ax^n - 16ax^{n-1} + \cdots$ and $S(p + q) = 8$. Example: $p = x^2 - 7x$, $q = x^2 - 9x + 22$ ($p - q = 2x - 22$, root $11$).
  * If $a \ne b$, then $\frac{7a - 9b}{a - b} = 11$, so $b = 2a$; $p + q = 3ax^n - 25ax^{n-1} + \cdots$ and $S(p + q) = \frac{25}{3}$. Example: $p = x - 7$, $q = 2x - 18$.
* **$n = m + 1$.** $p - q = ax^n - (7a + b)x^{n-1} + \cdots$, so $7 + \frac ba = 11$, $b = 4a$, and $p + q = ax^n - 3ax^{n-1} + \cdots$: $S(p + q) = 3$. Example: $p = x^2 - 7x$, $q = 4x - 36$.
* **$m = n + 1$.** $p - q = -bx^m + (9b + a)x^{m-1} + \cdots$, so $\frac{9b + a}{b} = 11$, $a = 2b$, and $p + q = bx^m - 7bx^{m-1} + \cdots$: $S(p + q) = 7$. Example: $p = 2x - 14$, $q = x^2 - 9x$.

(Check one example: $p = x^2 - 7x$, $q = 4x - 36$: $p - q = x^2 - 11x + 36$ has root sum $11$ and $p + q = x^2 - 3x - 36$ has root sum $3$.)

**Answer: $S(p + q) \in \left\{3, 7, 8, \tfrac{25}{3}\right\}$**

usamts-2020-r2-04.title: Ratio lemma on two triangles
usamts-2020-r2-04.body:
Write $A, B, C$ for the angles of the triangle; $AB < AC$ means $C < B$. Let $X = CH \cap AT$ and $Y = CH \cap AO$ (configuration as in the figure). We show that always
$$\frac{AX}{XT} = \frac{HY}{YC},$$
which proves the claim, since $AX = XT$ is given.

**Ratio lemma.** If $D$ lies on side $UV$ of $\triangle WUV$, then $\frac{UD}{DV} = \frac{WU\sin\angle UWD}{WV\sin\angle DWV}$. (Law of sines in $\triangle WUD$ and $\triangle WDV$, using $\sin\angle WDU = \sin\angle WDV$.)

**Angles we need.**

* Tangent–chord: $\angle TAB = \angle ACB = C$, so $\angle TAC = A + C = 180^\circ - B$, and the exterior angle at $B$ in $\triangle ABT$ gives $\angle ATC = B - C$.
* $CH \perp AB$, so $\angle ACH = 90^\circ - A$ and $\angle HCB = 90^\circ - B$.
* $AH \perp BC$ gives $\angle HAC = 90^\circ - C$, while $\angle OAC = 90^\circ - B$ (isosceles $\triangle OAC$ with apex angle $2B$). Hence $\angle HAY = \angle HAC - \angle OAC = B - C$ and $\angle YAC = 90^\circ - B$.
* In $\triangle AHC$: $\angle AHC = 180^\circ - (90^\circ - C) - (90^\circ - A) = A + C$.

**Triangle $CAT$ with cevian $CX$:**
$$\frac{AX}{XT} = \frac{CA\sin\angle ACX}{CT\sin\angle XCT} = \frac{\sin\angle ATC}{\sin\angle TAC}\cdot\frac{\cos A}{\cos B} = \frac{\sin(B - C)}{\sin B}\cdot\frac{\cos A}{\cos B},$$
using $\frac{CA}{CT} = \frac{\sin\angle ATC}{\sin\angle TAC}$ (law of sines) and $\sin(180^\circ - B) = \sin B$.

**Triangle $AHC$ with cevian $AY$:**
$$\frac{HY}{YC} = \frac{AH\sin\angle HAY}{AC\sin\angle YAC} = \frac{\sin\angle ACH}{\sin\angle AHC}\cdot\frac{\sin(B - C)}{\cos B} = \frac{\cos A}{\sin(A + C)}\cdot\frac{\sin(B - C)}{\cos B},$$
and $\sin(A + C) = \sin B$. The two expressions agree, so $\frac{AX}{XT} = \frac{HY}{YC}$. With $AX = XT$ we get $HY = YC$: line $AO$ passes through the midpoint of $CH$. ∎

usamts-2020-r2-04.title: Complex numbers (outline of the official computation)
usamts-2020-r2-04.body:
Put the circumcircle as the unit circle, so $o = 0$, $h = a + b + c$, $\bar a = 1/a$, etc. The tangent at $a$ is $z + a^2\bar z = 2a$ and line $BC$ is $z + bc\bar z = b + c$; solving gives
$$t = \frac{a^2(b + c) - 2abc}{a^2 - bc}.$$
Let $x = \frac{a + t}{2}$ be the midpoint of $AT$ and $y = \frac{c + h}{2} = \frac{a + b + 2c}{2}$ the midpoint of $CH$. The hypothesis says $\frac{x - c}{h - c} = \frac{a + t - 2c}{2(a + b)}$ is real; equating it with its conjugate and simplifying (a factor $a - c \ne 0$ cancels) gives
$$2bc^2 + b^2c = 2a^2b + a^2c,\quad\text{i.e.}\quad \frac{b + 2c}{a} = \frac{a(2b + c)}{bc} = \overline{\left(\frac{b + 2c}{a}\right)}.$$
So $\frac{b + 2c}{a}$ is real, hence so is $\frac{y - o}{a - o} = \frac{a + b + 2c}{2a} = \frac12 + \frac{b + 2c}{2a}$. Therefore $A$, $O$, $Y$ are collinear: $AO$ passes through the midpoint of $CH$. ∎

usamts-2020-r2-05.title: Work modulo powers of 2
usamts-2020-r2-05.body:
We prove it with $2020$ replaced by any positive integer $k$. Let $f(n)$ be the number obtained from $5^k n$ by replacing each decimal digit with its parity and reading the result in binary; so $a_{i+1} = f(a_i)$. Bit $j$ of $f(n)$ is the parity of the decimal digit of $5^k n$ in place $10^j$.

**Lemma 1.** For $0 \le b \le k$ and all $n$:
(a) $f(n + 2^b) \equiv f(n) + 2^b \pmod{2^{b+1}}$; (b) $f(n + 2^{b+1}) \equiv f(n) \pmod{2^{b+1}}$.

*Proof.* (a) $5^k(n + 2^b) = 5^k n + 10^b\cdot 5^{k-b}$, and $5^{k-b}$ is odd. Adding $10^b\cdot(\text{odd})$ leaves the last $b$ digits unchanged, and (no carry arrives from below) changes the digit in place $10^b$ by an odd amount mod $10$, flipping its parity. So $f$ keeps bits $0, \dots, b-1$ and flips bit $b$, which changes it by $\pm 2^b \equiv 2^b \pmod{2^{b+1}}$.
(b) Now we add $10^b\cdot 2\cdot 5^{k-b}$, an even number times $10^b$: the last $b$ digits are unchanged and the digit in place $10^b$ changes by an even amount, so bits $0, \dots, b$ of $f$ are unchanged. $\square$

By (b), $f$ is well defined modulo $2^{b+1}$ for $b \le k$: $x \equiv y \pmod{2^{b+1}}$ implies $f(x) \equiv f(y)$. Also $f(n) \equiv n \pmod 2$ (the last digit of $5^k n$ has the parity of $n$).

**Lemma 2.** For $0 \le b \le k$ and all $i$: $a_i \equiv a_{i + 2^b} \pmod{2^{b+1}}$.

*Proof by induction on $b$.* For $b = 0$: $a_{i+1} = f(a_i) \equiv a_i \pmod 2$. Suppose it holds for $b - 1$, so $a_1 \equiv a_{1 + 2^{b-1}} \pmod{2^b}$. Modulo $2^{b+1}$ either
* $a_1 \equiv a_{1 + 2^{b-1}}$: applying the well-defined $f$ repeatedly, $a_i \equiv a_{i + 2^{b-1}}$ for all $i$, hence $a_i \equiv a_{i + 2^{b-1}} \equiv a_{i + 2^b}$; or
* $a_1 \equiv a_{1 + 2^{b-1}} + 2^b$: by Lemma 1(a) and well-definedness, $a_i \equiv a_{i + 2^{b-1}} + 2^b$ for all $i$, so $a_i \equiv a_{i + 2^b} + 2\cdot 2^b \equiv a_{i + 2^b}$. $\square$

**Lemma 3.** $f(n) < \max(n, 2^{k+1})$ for every $n \ge 0$.

*Proof.* If $n < 2^k\cdot 10$, then $5^k n < 10^{k+1}$ has at most $k + 1$ digits, so $f(n) < 2^{k+1}$. Otherwise pick $d \ge 1$ with $2^k 10^d \le n < 2^k 10^{d+1}$; then $5^k n < 10^{k + d + 1}$, so $f(n) < 2^{k + d + 1} < 2^k\cdot 10^d \le n$ (as $2^{d+1} < 10^d$ for $d \ge 1$). $\square$

**Finish.** By Lemma 3 the sequence strictly decreases while $a_i \ge 2^{k+1}$, so some $a_N < 2^{k+1}$, and then all later terms stay below $2^{k+1}$. For $i \ge N$, Lemma 2 with $b = k$ gives $a_i \equiv a_{i + 2^k} \pmod{2^{k+1}}$ with both numbers in $[0, 2^{k+1})$, so $a_i = a_{i + 2^k}$. With $k = 2020$ this is the claim. ∎
